title: Presenting Research
subtitle: Structure a research talk, comment on visual aids with precision, and handle a difficult question with composure

lessons.title: Structurer une présentation
lessons.description: Build the architecture of a research presentation — a hook that earns attention, a plan that is announced and honoured, and a conclusion that lands.

blocks.heading: L'accroche et l'annonce du plan
blocks.body: A research presentation is judged within its first thirty seconds: a flat opening ('Aujourd'hui, je vais parler de...') loses the audience before the first slide. A strong 'accroche' — a striking fact, a pointed question, a brief anecdote — earns the right to be heard, and it must lead directly into the 'problématique', the precise question the whole talk exists to answer. Once the audience knows what question is at stake, announcing the plan tells them how the answer will unfold, so that nothing that follows feels arbitrary.

examples.french: Imaginez que la moitié des données que vous consultez chaque jour aient été mal étiquetées : c'est exactement ce que nous avons découvert.
examples.english: Imagine that half the data you consult every day had been mislabelled: that is exactly what we discovered.

examples.french: Notre problématique est simple à formuler, bien plus difficile à trancher : la précocité d'un diagnostic compense-t-elle son incertitude ?
examples.english: Our central question is simple to state, far harder to settle: does the earliness of a diagnosis compensate for its uncertainty?

examples.french: Je présenterai d'abord notre méthode, puis nos résultats, avant de discuter leurs limites.
examples.english: I will first present our method, then our results, before discussing their limitations.

examples.french: Cette présentation s'articule en trois temps : le contexte, la démonstration, et les pistes qu'elle ouvre.
examples.english: This presentation unfolds in three stages: the context, the demonstration, and the avenues it opens up.

blocks.tip: Write your accroche last, after the rest of the talk is fixed — it is far easier to find the one striking fact that captures a finished argument than to write a hook for an argument you have not yet built.

blocks.heading: Les articulateurs logiques : faire progresser l'exposé
blocks.body: Between the announced plan and the conclusion, a presentation must visibly move: each new point should be marked by a discourse connector that tells the audience exactly where they are in the argument. 'Dans un premier temps' opens the first movement; 'par la suite' or 'ensuite' carries it forward; 'quant à' pivots cleanly to a related but distinct point; 'enchaîner' names the very skill of moving from one idea to the next without a jarring gap.

examples.french: Dans un premier temps, je situerai notre étude par rapport aux travaux existants.
examples.english: First of all, I will situate our study in relation to existing work.

examples.french: Par la suite, nous verrons comment ce résultat a été obtenu, puis ce qu'il implique.
examples.english: Subsequently, we will see how this result was obtained, and then what it implies.

examples.french: Quant à la deuxième hypothèse, elle mérite un traitement à part.
examples.english: As for the second hypothesis, it deserves separate treatment.

examples.french: Un bon orateur enchaîne les parties sans jamais perdre son auditoire en chemin.
examples.english: A good speaker moves from one part to the next without ever losing the audience along the way.

blocks.tip: Say the connector out loud a beat before the idea it introduces — a short pause after 'quant à' or 'dans un premier temps' signals the shift more clearly than rushing the two together.

blocks.heading: La conclusion : synthétiser sans répéter
blocks.body: A weak conclusion simply restates the introduction in the past tense; a strong one performs a genuine synthesis, pulling the separate threads of the talk into a single, memorable message, then opening — briefly — onto what the research still leaves unresolved. 'Pour conclure' and 'en guise de conclusion' both signal the closing movement, but the content that follows must add value, not just announce that the end has arrived.

examples.french: Pour conclure, retenons un seul message : la méthode compte autant que le résultat.
examples.english: To conclude, let us retain a single message: the method matters as much as the result.

examples.french: En guise de conclusion, j'aimerais ouvrir sur une question que nos données ne permettent pas encore de trancher.
examples.english: By way of conclusion, I would like to open onto a question our data cannot yet settle.

examples.french: Cette synthèse ne prétend pas clore le débat ; elle propose un point d'appui pour la suite.
examples.english: This synthesis does not claim to close the debate; it offers a foothold for what comes next.

examples.french: Résumez la démonstration, pas le plan : votre auditoire a suivi le plan, il attend maintenant ce qu'il faut en retenir.
examples.english: Sum up the demonstration, not the outline: your audience has followed the outline, it is now waiting to hear what to take away from it.

blocks.tip: Draft your conclusion's single key message in one sentence before you finish the slides — if you cannot state it in one sentence, the talk itself likely needs one more round of hierarchising.

blocks.heading: La nominalisation : condenser l'exposé dans un registre académique
blocks.body: Formal spoken presentations lean heavily on nominalisation — turning a verb into a noun — because a nominalised clause packs the same information into fewer, weightier words and lets the speaker treat an action as a stable object to refer back to across several slides. 'Les données ont été analysées' becomes 'l'analyse des données'; 'la méthode a évolué' becomes 'l'évolution de la méthode'. The technique also lets a speaker leave the agent unstated when it is irrelevant to the point being made.

examples.french: Après la collecte des données, nous avons procédé à leur analyse.
examples.english: After the collection of the data, we proceeded to their analysis.

examples.french: L'évolution de la méthode s'explique par trois contraintes que je vais détailler.
examples.english: The evolution of the method is explained by three constraints I will detail.

examples.french: La validation des résultats a pris plus de temps que leur obtention.
examples.english: The validation of the results took longer than obtaining them.

examples.french: Plutôt que de dire « nous avons interprété les résultats avec prudence », préférez « l'interprétation des résultats appelle à la prudence ».
examples.english: Rather than saying 'we interpreted the results cautiously', prefer 'the interpretation of the results calls for caution'.

blocks.tip: Draft each slide's key sentence twice, once with a verb and once nominalised, then read both aloud — the nominalised version usually sounds more like a research talk, but only keep it if it stays clear, since overusing nominalisation can make a sentence feel abstract and hard to follow.

blocks.heading: Les tournures de l'oral formel : cohortatif, impersonnel, infinitif d'instruction
blocks.body: Live presentations rely on a small set of grammatical devices to guide the audience through the talk in real time. The first-person plural imperative ('Voyons maintenant...', 'Passons à...') includes the audience in the movement of thought without singling anyone out. Impersonal constructions ('il convient de', 'il importe de', 'il s'agit de') state a step formally, without an explicit subject. The bare infinitive, finally, works as a spoken instruction to oneself and the audience alike, common in structuring an oral account.

examples.french: Voyons maintenant comment ce résultat a été obtenu.
examples.english: Let us now see how this result was obtained.

examples.french: Passons à présent à la deuxième partie de notre démonstration.
examples.english: Let us now move on to the second part of our demonstration.

examples.french: Il convient de préciser que cet échantillon reste limité.
examples.english: It should be noted that this sample remains limited.

examples.french: Rappeler d'abord le contexte, présenter ensuite la méthode : voilà comment procéder.
examples.english: First recall the context, then present the method: that is how to proceed.

blocks.tip: Reserve the cohortative 'nous' ('voyons', 'passons') for moving between sections, and the impersonal 'il convient de' for stating a caveat or a rule — mixing the two registers within the same sentence tends to sound stilted rather than formal.

items.prompt: Announce that your talk unfolds in three stages: context, demonstration, and the avenues it opens up.
items.french: Cette présentation s'articule en trois temps : le contexte, la démonstration, et les pistes qu'elle ouvre.
items.english: This presentation unfolds in three stages: the context, the demonstration, and the avenues it opens up.
items.tip: Place a short pause after each of the three nouns — the rhythm itself signals the three-part structure before the words do.

items.prompt: Signal that you are moving to the second part of your demonstration.

passages.title: Transcription d'un exposé : « Le mythe du multitâche »
passages.french:
Imaginez que la moitié des tâches que vous croyez accomplir en parallèle soient en réalité traitées l'une après l'autre, à toute vitesse, sans que vous vous en rendiez compte : c'est exactement ce que notre étude a révélé.
Notre problématique est simple à formuler, bien plus difficile à trancher : le multitâche numérique améliore-t-il vraiment la productivité, ou ne fait-il que déplacer la fatigue ?
Cette présentation s'articule en trois temps : le contexte de la recherche, la méthode employée, puis les résultats et leurs limites.
Dans un premier temps, situons notre étude par rapport aux travaux existants, qui restaient jusqu'ici largement contradictoires.
Nous avons suivi deux cents volontaires pendant six semaines, en alternant des journées de travail concentré et des journées de travail fragmenté par des notifications.
Par la suite, l'analyse des données a montré un écart net : la fragmentation de l'attention allonge le temps nécessaire à chaque tâche de près d'un tiers.
Quant à la sensation subjective de productivité, elle suit une courbe inverse à la productivité réelle, ce qui explique en partie pourquoi le mythe persiste.
Il convient de préciser que notre échantillon reste limité à un seul secteur professionnel, ce qui appelle une réplique plus large avant toute généralisation.
Pour conclure, retenons un seul message : la concentration ininterrompue reste, à ce jour, la ressource la plus rare et la plus précieuse de nos organisations.
En guise d'ouverture, une question demeure entière : nos outils numériques peuvent-ils être redessinés pour protéger cette ressource, plutôt que pour la disperser ?
La séance de questions qui a suivi cet exposé a duré presque aussi longtemps que la présentation elle-même.
passages.english:
Imagine that half the tasks you believe you are performing in parallel are actually processed one after another, at high speed, without your realising it: that is exactly what our study revealed.
Our central question is simple to state, far harder to settle: does digital multitasking really improve productivity, or does it merely displace fatigue?
This presentation unfolds in three stages: the research context, the method used, then the results and their limitations.
First of all, let us situate our study in relation to existing work, which had until now remained largely contradictory.
We followed two hundred volunteers for six weeks, alternating days of focused work with days of work fragmented by notifications.
Subsequently, the analysis of the data showed a clear gap: the fragmentation of attention lengthens the time needed for each task by nearly a third.
As for the subjective feeling of productivity, it follows a curve inverse to actual productivity, which partly explains why the myth persists.
It should be noted that our sample remains limited to a single professional sector, which calls for a larger replication before any generalisation.
To conclude, let us retain a single message: uninterrupted concentration remains, to this day, the rarest and most precious resource in our organisations.
By way of an opening, one question remains wide open: can our digital tools be redesigned to protect this resource, rather than to scatter it?
The question session that followed this talk lasted almost as long as the presentation itself.

lessons.title: Le support visuel
lessons.description: Design slides that support the spoken argument rather than duplicate it, and learn the precise vocabulary for commenting on a chart in real time.

blocks.heading: Le support visuel : soutenir le propos, jamais le remplacer
blocks.body: A slide exists to support what the speaker is saying, not to replace it: a slide crowded with full sentences forces the audience to choose between reading and listening, and they invariably read. The soundest habit is to strip each slide down to a title, an image or a chart, and at most a handful of words, then say aloud everything that a written paragraph would otherwise have carried.

examples.french: Un support visuel surchargé de texte détourne l'attention du discours lui-même.
examples.english: A visual aid overloaded with text diverts attention away from the talk itself.

examples.french: Épurez chaque diapositive jusqu'à ce qu'elle ne porte plus qu'une seule idée.
examples.english: Strip each slide down until it carries only a single idea.

examples.french: Une bonne infographie remplace un paragraphe entier d'explications.
examples.english: A good infographic replaces an entire paragraph of explanations.

examples.french: La lisibilité d'une diapositive se juge depuis le fond de la salle, pas depuis l'écran de l'orateur.
examples.english: A slide's readability is judged from the back of the room, not from the speaker's own screen.

blocks.tip: Apply a strict six-second test to every slide: if the audience cannot grasp its core point within six seconds of it appearing, it needs to be simplified further.

blocks.heading: Décrire un graphique : la structure de la phrase descriptive
blocks.body: Commenting on a chart in French follows a small set of recurring frames: 'ce graphique montre / illustre / représente' introduces what the chart depicts; 'on constate que' and 'il apparaît que' introduce the interpretation drawn from it; a rise or fall is described with 'la hausse de' or 'la baisse de' followed by a figure, and 'par rapport à' anchors that figure against a comparison point. Mastering these frames lets a speaker move fluidly between showing data and interpreting it.

examples.french: Ce graphique illustre l'évolution du taux de réponse sur cinq ans.
examples.english: This chart illustrates the evolution of the response rate over five years.

examples.french: On constate une hausse de douze points par rapport à l'année précédente.
examples.english: We observe a rise of twelve points compared with the previous year.

examples.french: Il apparaît que la tendance s'inverse à partir du troisième trimestre.
examples.english: It appears that the trend reverses from the third quarter onwards.

examples.french: L'axe des abscisses représente le temps ; l'axe des ordonnées, le pourcentage de réponses.
examples.english: The x-axis represents time; the y-axis, the percentage of responses.

blocks.tip: Point to the axis or the curve you are describing a fraction of a second before naming it in speech — the gesture and the word should land almost together, not the word well after the gesture.

blocks.heading: Naviguer et commenter en direct : les gestes du support visuel
blocks.body: Handling slides live is itself a skill: a speaker who fumbles between slides, apologises for a cluttered graph, or reads a caption word for word breaks the flow of the talk. Clean transitions between slides, a confident pointer or cursor, and a habit of paraphrasing rather than reading the legend all keep the audience's attention on the argument rather than on the mechanics of the presentation.

examples.french: Je fais défiler les diapositives lentement pour laisser le temps de lire le graphique.
examples.english: I scroll through the slides slowly to leave time to read the chart.

examples.french: Ce nuage de points met en évidence une corrélation que le tableau seul ne montrait pas.
examples.english: This scatter plot highlights a correlation that the table alone did not show.

examples.french: La légende précise l'unité de mesure utilisée pour chaque courbe.
examples.english: The legend specifies the unit of measurement used for each curve.

examples.french: Plutôt que de lire la légende, commentez-la avec vos propres mots.
examples.english: Rather than reading the legend aloud, comment on it in your own words.

blocks.tip: Rehearse the exact sentence you will say while a chart is on screen — improvising the commentary live is when speakers most often slip into reading the slide word for word.

blocks.heading: Les tournures impersonnelles et passives pour décrire un support visuel
blocks.body: Describing a chart in careful spoken French favours structures that foreground the data rather than the speaker: the passive voice ('les résultats sont représentés par...') and impersonal formulas ('il apparaît que', 'on constate que', 'il ressort de ce graphique que') let the chart itself seem to speak. These structures are not mere politeness — they mark a register in which the presenter reports what the data show rather than what the presenter personally believes.

examples.french: Les résultats sont représentés par une courbe continue, les prévisions par une ligne pointillée.
examples.english: The results are represented by a solid line, the forecasts by a dotted line.

examples.french: Il ressort de ce graphique que les deux groupes convergent après la dixième semaine.
examples.english: It emerges from this chart that the two groups converge after the tenth week.

examples.french: On constate que l'écart se resserre à mesure que l'échantillon grandit.
examples.english: We observe that the gap narrows as the sample grows.

examples.french: Ces données ont été collectées sur douze mois, puis agrégées par trimestre.
examples.english: This data was collected over twelve months, then aggregated by quarter.

blocks.tip: Alternate a passive sentence with an impersonal one rather than repeating the same frame for every chart — 'les résultats sont représentés par...' followed later by 'il apparaît que...' keeps the commentary from sounding mechanical.

blocks.heading: Comparer et situer un chiffre : structures de la proportion
blocks.body: A number alone rarely means much to an audience; it needs a comparison point to become informative. 'Par rapport à' anchors a figure against an earlier one; 'contre' contrasts two figures directly; 'soit' introduces a figure restated in a more readable form (a percentage recast as a fraction, for instance); and comparative structures ('deux fois plus que', 'trois fois moins que') let a speaker convey magnitude instantly, without forcing the audience to do the arithmetic themselves.

examples.french: Ce chiffre progresse de six points par rapport à l'an dernier.
examples.english: This figure rises by six points compared with last year.

examples.french: Soixante-douze pour cent des répondants contre vingt-huit pour cent l'an dernier.
examples.english: Seventy-two percent of respondents, against twenty-eight percent last year.

examples.french: Soit environ un répondant sur trois, un chiffre à retenir.
examples.english: That is, roughly one respondent in three, a figure worth remembering.

examples.french: Le second groupe a mis deux fois plus de temps à terminer la tâche.
examples.english: The second group took twice as long to finish the task.

blocks.tip: Do the arithmetic for the audience before you speak, not while speaking — announcing 'soit environ un sur trois' immediately after a percentage is far clearer than leaving listeners to convert the figure themselves.

passages.title: Transcription d'un exposé : commenter le graphique central
passages.french:
Passons à présent au graphique qui résume, à lui seul, l'essentiel de notre démonstration.
L'axe des abscisses représente le temps écoulé depuis le lancement de l'étude ; l'axe des ordonnées, le pourcentage de participants encore actifs.
Comme le montre ce graphique, la courbe bleue, celle du groupe suivi sans interruption, reste stable autour de quatre-vingts pour cent.
La courbe orange, elle, décrit un tout autre parcours : on constate une baisse continue à partir de la sixième semaine.
Il apparaît que cet écart, de vingt-deux points au terme de l'étude, ne peut s'expliquer par le hasard de l'échantillonnage.
La légende précise l'unité de mesure utilisée pour chaque courbe, afin d'éviter toute confusion entre les deux échelles.
Ce nuage de points, en bas de la diapositive, met en évidence une corrélation que le tableau de données seul ne montrait pas.
Nous avons volontairement épuré cette diapositive : aucune phrase complète, seulement le graphique, ses deux courbes, et une légende de trois mots.
Un tel support visuel se lit en six secondes ; le reste, c'est à moi de le dire, pas à la diapositive de l'écrire.
Soixante-douze pour cent des participants du premier groupe ont terminé l'étude, soit environ deux sur trois — un chiffre à retenir avant de passer à la suite.
Je fais défiler la diapositive suivante, qui replace ce résultat dans le contexte plus large de la littérature existante.
passages.english:
Let us now move to the chart that alone sums up the essence of our demonstration.
The x-axis represents the time elapsed since the start of the study; the y-axis, the percentage of participants still active.
As this chart shows, the blue curve, that of the group followed without interruption, stays stable around eighty percent.
The orange curve, on the other hand, describes a very different path: we observe a continuous decline starting from the sixth week.
It appears that this gap, twenty-two points by the end of the study, cannot be explained by chance in the sampling.
The legend specifies the unit of measurement used for each curve, to avoid any confusion between the two scales.
This scatter plot, at the bottom of the slide, highlights a correlation that the data table alone did not show.
We deliberately stripped this slide down: no complete sentences, only the chart, its two curves, and a three-word legend.
Such a visual aid can be read in six seconds; the rest is for me to say, not for the slide to write.
Seventy-two percent of the participants in the first group completed the study, that is, roughly two out of three — a figure worth remembering before we move on.
I click through to the next slide, which places this result within the broader context of the existing literature.

lessons.title: Gérer les questions difficiles
lessons.description: Face a hostile or destabilising question in a Q&A session without losing composure — reformulate, concede where warranted, and answer with precision.

blocks.heading: La séance de questions : un exercice à part entière
blocks.body: The question session is not an afterthought to a presentation; for many listeners it is the moment that reveals whether the speaker truly masters the subject. A trick question, a hostile objection, or a question the speaker simply cannot answer will all arise sooner or later, and the way they are handled matters as much as the talk itself. The first rule is procedural: listen to the whole question before responding, even when it is long or clearly leading somewhere uncomfortable.

examples.french: La séance de questions qui a suivi cet exposé a duré presque aussi longtemps que la présentation elle-même.
examples.english: The question session that followed this talk lasted almost as long as the presentation itself.

examples.french: Une question piège n'attend pas une réponse, elle attend une hésitation.
examples.english: A trick question does not expect an answer, it expects a hesitation.

examples.french: Écoutez la question jusqu'au bout avant de répondre, même si elle semble déjà vous mener où vous ne voulez pas aller.
examples.english: Listen to the question in full before answering, even if it already seems to be leading you somewhere you do not want to go.

examples.french: Le modérateur a donné la parole à trois personnes avant de clore la séance de questions.
examples.english: The moderator gave the floor to three people before closing the question session.

blocks.tip: Pause visibly for one full second after a difficult question before answering — that brief silence reads as composure, not as a sign that you are struggling.

blocks.heading: Reformuler, concéder, nuancer : les trois réflexes de la réponse solide
blocks.body: A strong answer to a difficult question rarely starts with a flat 'oui' or 'non'. Reformulating the question first buys a moment to think and confirms that the speaker has understood it correctly; conceding a valid point, when one exists, disarms the questioner before the answer moves on; and nuancing the final response — refusing a false binary choice — usually reflects the real state of the evidence better than a blunt answer would.

examples.french: Je reformule votre question autrement : vous demandez si nos résultats resteraient valables sur un échantillon plus large ?
examples.english: Let me rephrase your question differently: are you asking whether our results would still hold on a larger sample?

examples.french: Je concède que notre échantillon reste limité ; c'est une limite que nous assumons pleinement.
examples.english: I concede that our sample remains limited; that is a limitation we fully acknowledge.

examples.french: Ma réponse mérite d'être nuancée : cela dépend largement du secteur considéré.
examples.english: My answer deserves to be qualified: it depends largely on the sector in question.

examples.french: Plutôt que d'éluder la question, admettons que ce point reste, à ce jour, non résolu.
examples.english: Rather than evading the question, let us admit that this point remains, to this day, unresolved.

blocks.tip: Reformulate only questions that are genuinely ambiguous or hostile — reformulating a clear, friendly question can come across as stalling rather than as careful listening.

blocks.heading: Garder le contrôle : ce qu'il ne faut jamais faire
blocks.body: Certain reflexes reliably damage a speaker's credibility during a question session: dodging the question outright ('botter en touche'), pretending to know an answer that one does not have, or becoming visibly defensive at the first sign of disagreement. The far stronger move, when a question genuinely exceeds what the research supports, is to recognise the limits of one's knowledge openly — an admission that, delivered calmly, tends to increase rather than damage credibility.

examples.french: Botter en touche sur une question de fond se remarque immédiatement, et se retient longtemps.
examples.english: Dodging a substantive question is noticed immediately, and remembered for a long time.

examples.french: Je n'ai pas de réponse définitive à cette question ; nos données ne permettent pas encore de trancher.
examples.english: I do not have a definitive answer to that question; our data do not yet allow us to settle it.

examples.french: Reconnaître ses limites, calmement, renforce la crédibilité plus qu'elle ne l'entame.
examples.english: Acknowledging one's limits, calmly, strengthens credibility rather than undermining it.

examples.french: Restez courtois même face à un contradicteur de mauvaise foi ; le public juge le ton autant que le contenu.
examples.english: Remain courteous even facing a challenger acting in bad faith; the audience judges the tone as much as the content.

blocks.tip: Prepare, in advance, a single honest sentence for the one question you most hope nobody asks — having it ready removes the temptation to dodge it in the moment.

blocks.heading: Concéder avant de nuancer : certes... mais / il est vrai que... néanmoins
blocks.body: The most persuasive way to answer a difficult objection is often to grant it something first: 'certes... mais' and 'il est vrai que... néanmoins' both open by conceding a real point before pivoting, with 'mais' or 'néanmoins', to the qualification that actually answers the challenge. This structure works because it shows the questioner they have been heard fairly, which makes the pivot that follows far more persuasive than a flat denial would be.

examples.french: Certes, notre échantillon est restreint, mais les effets observés restent cohérents avec la littérature existante.
examples.english: Certainly, our sample is small, but the effects observed remain consistent with the existing literature.

examples.french: Il est vrai que la méthode comporte des limites ; néanmoins, elle reste la plus rigoureuse disponible à ce jour.
examples.english: It is true that the method has limitations; nevertheless, it remains the most rigorous one available to date.

examples.french: Vous avez raison sur ce point précis ; cela ne remet cependant pas en cause la conclusion générale.
examples.english: You are right about this specific point; that does not, however, call the overall conclusion into question.

examples.french: Concédons que la question reste ouverte, tout en rappelant ce que nos données permettent déjà d'affirmer.
examples.english: Let us concede that the question remains open, while recalling what our data already allow us to state.

blocks.tip: Never let the concession run longer than the pivot that follows it — a concession that outweighs the 'mais' or 'néanmoins' leaves the audience remembering the objection, not the answer.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel d'atténuation : répondre sans trop s'avancer
blocks.body: The conditional mood softens a claim without weakening it into vagueness: 'il conviendrait de', 'je dirais que', 'cela pourrait s'expliquer par' all present an answer as considered and provisional rather than as a flat assertion the speaker cannot fully back. This register is especially useful when a question pushes toward a conclusion the data do not yet fully support — the conditional lets the speaker answer honestly without either overclaiming or refusing to engage.

examples.french: Je dirais que le facteur principal reste, à ce stade, le temps d'exposition.
examples.english: I would say that the main factor remains, at this stage, exposure time.

examples.french: Cela pourrait s'expliquer par un biais de sélection, mais nous ne pouvons pas l'affirmer avec certitude.
examples.english: This could be explained by a selection bias, but we cannot state it with certainty.

examples.french: Il conviendrait de mener une étude complémentaire avant de trancher définitivement.
examples.english: A follow-up study would be advisable before settling the matter definitively.

examples.french: On pourrait avancer que ce résultat s'applique à d'autres contextes ; ce serait toutefois prématuré.
examples.english: One might suggest that this result applies to other contexts; that would, however, be premature.

blocks.tip: Pair a conditional answer with one concrete fact you can state with certainty — the conditional signals honest caution, but a bare hedge with nothing solid behind it can start to sound evasive rather than careful.

items.tip: End on a genuinely rising, questioning intonation — this is a check for understanding, not a rhetorical restatement.

items.english: Certainly, our sample is small, but the effects observed remain consistent with the existing literature.
items.tip: Keep 'certes' brief and let the weight of the sentence fall after 'mais' — the concession should sound genuine but short.

items.prompt: Admit calmly that you do not have a definitive answer, since the data cannot yet settle the question.
items.french: Je n'ai pas de réponse définitive à cette question ; nos données ne permettent pas encore de trancher.
items.english: I do not have a definitive answer to that question; our data do not yet allow us to settle it.
items.tip: Keep your tone level and unhurried throughout — this sentence works only if it sounds like calm honesty, not like an apology.

passages.title: Transcription d'une séance de questions
passages.french:
Le modérateur : Nous avons le temps pour quelques questions. Vous, au fond de la salle.
Un participant : Vos résultats me semblent trop beaux pour être vrais. N'avez-vous pas simplement sélectionné les données qui vous arrangeaient ?
La conférencière : Je reformule votre question autrement : vous demandez si nous avons pratiqué une forme de sélection des données a posteriori ?
Le participant : Exactement.
La conférencière : C'est une objection légitime, et je vous en remercie. Il est vrai que ce risque existe dans toute étude de ce type ; néanmoins, notre protocole a été déposé et figé avant la collecte, précisément pour l'écarter.
Un deuxième participant : Certes, mais votre échantillon reste très restreint. Comment peut-on généraliser à partir de deux cents personnes ?
La conférencière : Vous avez raison sur ce point précis ; cela ne remet cependant pas en cause la cohérence du résultat avec la littérature existante, que nous avons largement citée.
Le modérateur : Une dernière question, brève si possible.
Une troisième participante : Que répondez-vous à ceux qui jugent votre méthode dépassée ?
La conférencière : Je n'ai pas de réponse définitive à cette critique ; je dirais simplement qu'aucune méthode n'est parfaite, et que la nôtre reste, à ce stade, la plus rigoureuse dont nous disposions.
Le modérateur : Merci à tous. Il est temps de clore la séance de questions ; notre invitée reste disponible ensuite, dans le couloir.
passages.english:
The moderator: We have time for a few questions. You, at the back of the room.
A participant: Your results seem too good to be true to me. Didn't you simply select the data that suited you?
The speaker: Let me rephrase your question differently: are you asking whether we practised a form of data selection after the fact?
The participant: Exactly.
The speaker: That is a legitimate objection, and I thank you for it. It is true that this risk exists in any study of this kind; nevertheless, our protocol was filed and locked before data collection, precisely to rule that out.
A second participant: Certainly, but your sample remains very small. How can one generalise from two hundred people?
The speaker: You are right about this specific point; that does not, however, call into question the result's consistency with the existing literature, which we cited extensively.
The moderator: One last question, brief if possible.
A third participant: What do you say to those who consider your method outdated?
The speaker: I do not have a definitive answer to that criticism; I would simply say that no method is perfect, and that ours remains, at this stage, the most rigorous one available to us.
The moderator: Thank you all. It is time to close the question session; our guest remains available afterwards, in the hallway.
